title: Chapter 18. Of the Rights of Sovereigns by Institution
paragraphs: A commonwealth is said to be instituted when a multitude of men agree, and covenant, every one with every one, that whatever man, or assembly of men, shall be given by the majority the right to present the person of them all (that is, to be their representative), every one — both those who voted for him and those who voted against him — shall authorise all the actions and judgements of that man, or assembly of men, as if they were his own; and that this is done to the end of living peaceably among themselves and being protected against other men.
From this institution of a commonwealth are derived all the rights and faculties of the man, or men, on whom sovereign power is conferred by the consent of the people assembled.

First, because they covenant, it is to be understood that they are not bound by any prior covenant to anything contrary to this. Consequently, those who have already instituted a commonwealth, being bound by covenant to own the actions and judgements of one man, cannot lawfully make a new covenant among themselves to be obedient to any other in any matter without his permission. And so the subjects of a monarch cannot, without his leave, cast off monarchy and return to the confusion of a disunited multitude; nor transfer the person of him who bears it to another man, or to another assembly of men. For they are bound, every man to every man, to own and be reputed the author of all that he who is already their sovereign shall do and judge fit to be done; so that if any one man dissents, all the rest would break their covenant made with that man, which is injustice. They have also each given the sovereignty to the one who bears their person; so if they depose him, they take from him what is his own — which is again injustice. Besides, if the man who attempts to depose his sovereign is killed, or punished by him for the attempt, he is the author of his own punishment, being by the institution the author of all his sovereign does. And since it is unjust for a man to do anything for which he may be punished by his own authority, he is also, on that count, unjust. As for those who have pretended, as ground for disobedience to their sovereign, a new covenant made not with men but with God — that too is unjust. There is no covenant with God except through the mediation of some person who represents God's person; and none does that but God's lieutenant, who holds sovereignty under God. But this pretence of covenant with God is so plain a lie, even in the consciences of those who claim it, that it is an act not only of an unjust but also of a vile and unmanly disposition.

Second, because the right of bearing the person of them all is given to the man they make sovereign by covenant only of one to another, and not of him to any of them, no breach of covenant on the part of the sovereign can occur; and consequently none of his subjects, by any pretence of forfeiture, can be freed from his subjection. That the one made sovereign makes no covenant with his subjects beforehand is clear: for he must make it either with the whole multitude as one party to the covenant, or he must make a separate covenant with each man. With the whole, as one party, is impossible: as yet they are not one person. And if he makes as many separate covenants as there are men, then those covenants, after he has the sovereignty, are void; because whatever act any one of them may claim as a breach of it is the act both of himself and of every other, being done in the person of each, and by the right of every one of them in particular. Besides, if any one or more of them allege a breach of a covenant made by the sovereign at his institution, and others — or one other subject, or the sovereign himself alone — deny that any such breach took place, there is in that case no judge to decide the controversy; it returns therefore to the sword, and every man recovers the right of protecting himself by his own strength — contrary to the design they had in the institution. It is therefore pointless to grant sovereignty by way of any prior covenant. The opinion that any monarch receives his power by covenant — that is, on conditions — comes from a failure to grasp this easy truth: that covenants, being only words and breath, have no force to oblige, contain, constrain, or protect any man except what they get from the public sword — that is, from the untied hands of that man, or that assembly, who has the sovereignty, whose actions are avowed by them all and performed by the strength of them all, united in him. But when an assembly of men is made sovereign, no one imagines that any such covenant has passed at the institution. No one is so foolish as to say, for example, that the people of Rome made a covenant with the Romans to hold the sovereignty on such and such conditions — which, not performed, would have allowed the Romans lawfully to depose the Roman people. That men do not see the reasoning to be the same in a monarchy as in a popular government comes from the ambition of some, who are kinder to the government of an assembly of which they may hope to be a part than to a monarchy, which they despair of ever enjoying.
Third: No man can without injustice protest against the institution of the sovereign declared by the majority.

Because the majority by their consenting voices have declared a sovereign, he who dissented must now consent with the rest — that is, he must be content to avow whatever actions the sovereign shall do, or else justly be destroyed by the rest. For if he voluntarily entered into the congregation of those who were assembled, he sufficiently showed by that his will (and so tacitly covenanted) to stand by what the majority should ordain; and therefore if he refuses to do so, or makes any protest against any of their decrees, he acts contrary to his covenant, and so unjustly. And whether he is of the congregation or not, and whether his consent is asked or not, he must either submit to their decrees or be left in the condition of war he was in before — in which he could, without injustice, be destroyed by any man whatever.

Fourth, because by this institution every subject is the author of all the actions and judgements of the sovereign so instituted, it follows that whatever the sovereign does cannot be an injury to any of his subjects, nor ought he to be accused by any of them of injustice. For he who does anything by another's authority does no injury to the one by whose authority he acts. But by this institution of a commonwealth, every particular man is the author of all that the sovereign does; and consequently the man who complains of injury from his sovereign complains of that of which he is himself the author, and therefore ought to accuse no one but himself — nor even himself of injury, since to do injury to oneself is impossible. It is true that those who have sovereign power may commit iniquity, but not injustice, or injury, in the proper meaning of those words.

Fifth, and as a consequence of what was last said, no man who has sovereign power can justly be put to death, or otherwise in any manner punished by his subjects. For since every subject is the author of his sovereign's actions, he would be punishing another for actions committed by himself.

And because the end of this institution is the peace and defence of them all, and whoever has the right to the end has the right to the means, it belongs by right to whatever man or assembly has the sovereignty to be the judge both of the means of peace and defence, and of the hindrances and disturbances of the same — and to do whatever he shall think necessary to be done, both beforehand for preserving peace and security (by preventing discord at home and hostility from abroad) and, when peace and security are lost, for recovering them. And therefore:

Sixth, it is annexed to the sovereignty to be the judge of which opinions and doctrines are hostile to peace and which conducive to it, and consequently on what occasions, how far, and what men are to be trusted in speaking to multitudes of people, and who shall examine the doctrines of all books before they are published. For the actions of men proceed from their opinions; and in the good governing of opinions consists the good governing of men's actions, in order to their peace and concord. And though in matters of doctrine nothing ought to be regarded but the truth, this is not at odds with regulating it for the sake of peace. For doctrine contrary to peace can no more be true than peace and concord can be against the law of nature. It is true that in a commonwealth, where through the negligence or unskillfulness of governors and teachers, false doctrines have come, over time, to be generally received, the opposite truths may be generally offensive. Yet the most sudden and rough thrusting in of a new truth that can be never breaks the peace; it only sometimes wakes the war. For those men who are so loosely governed that they dare take up arms to defend or introduce an opinion are already in war; their condition is not peace but only a cessation of arms for fear of one another; and they live, as it were, perpetually on the verge of battle. It belongs therefore to the holder of sovereign power to be the judge, or to appoint all judges, of opinions and doctrines — as a thing necessary to peace, and to prevent discord and civil war.
Seventh: The right to make the rules by which each subject may know what is so much his own that no other subject may, without injustice, take it from him.

Annexed to the sovereignty is the whole power of prescribing the rules by which each man may know what goods he may enjoy, and what actions he may do, without being molested by any of his fellow subjects. And this is what men call property. For before the constitution of sovereign power (as has already been shown), all men had a right to all things; which necessarily causes war. And so this property, being necessary to peace and depending on sovereign power, is the act of that power, in the service of the public peace. These rules of property (or meum and tuum), and of good, evil, lawful, and unlawful in the actions of subjects, are the civil laws — that is, the laws of each commonwealth in particular; though the name 'civil law' is now restricted to the ancient civil laws of the city of Rome, which, being the head of a great part of the world, had laws which in our regions at that time were the civil law.

Eighth, annexed to the sovereignty is the right of judicature — that is, of hearing and deciding all controversies that may arise about law, whether civil or natural, or about fact. For without the decision of controversies, there is no protection of one subject against the injuries of another; the laws concerning meum and tuum are in vain; and each man is left, by the natural and necessary appetite for his own preservation, with the right of protecting himself by his private strength — which is the condition of war, and contrary to the end for which every commonwealth is instituted.

Ninth, annexed to the sovereignty is the right of making war and peace with other nations and commonwealths — that is, of judging when it is for the public good, and how great a force should be assembled, armed, and paid for that end, and of levying money on the subjects to cover the expenses. For the power by which the people are to be defended consists in their armies; and the strength of an army consists in the union of their strength under one command; and that command the sovereign by institution accordingly has — because command of the militia, even without any further institution, makes whoever has it sovereign. So whoever may be made general of an army, the one who has the sovereign power is always generalissimo.

Tenth, annexed to the sovereignty is the choosing of all counsellors, ministers, magistrates, and officers, in peace and in war. For since the sovereign is charged with the end — namely common peace and defence — he is understood to have the power to use such means as he shall think most fit for discharging it.
Eleventh: And of rewarding and punishing, and that (where no prior law has fixed the measure of it) at his own discretion.

To the sovereign is committed the power of rewarding with riches or honour, and of punishing with corporal or financial penalties, or with ignominy, every subject according to the law he has already made — or, where no law has been made, according as he shall judge most to conduce to encouraging men to serve the commonwealth, or to deterring them from doing it disservice.

Last, considering what values men are naturally apt to set on themselves, what respect they look for from others, and how little they value other men — from which there continually arise among them rivalry, quarrels, factions, and at last war, to the destruction of one another and the diminishing of their strength against a common enemy — it is necessary that there be laws of honour, and a public rate of worth for such men as have deserved, or are able to deserve well of the commonwealth; and that there be force in someone's hands to put those laws into execution. But it has already been shown that not only the whole militia, or armed force of the commonwealth, but also the judicature of all controversies, is annexed to the sovereignty. To the sovereign therefore it also belongs to give titles of honour, and to appoint what order of place and dignity each man shall hold, and what signs of respect men shall give to one another in public or private meetings.

These are the rights that make up the essence of sovereignty, and which are the marks by which a man may discern in which man, or assembly of men, the sovereign power is placed and resides. For these rights cannot be transferred and cannot be separated. The power to coin money; to dispose of the estate and persons of infant heirs; to have pre-emption in markets; and all other statute prerogatives may be transferred away by the sovereign, and yet the power to protect his subjects be retained. But if he transfers the militia, he retains the judicature in vain, for want of execution of the laws. Or if he grants away the power of raising money, the militia is in vain. Or if he gives away the government of doctrines, men will be frightened into rebellion by fear of spirits. And so if we consider any one of the said rights, we shall at once see that the holding of all the rest will produce no effect in preserving peace and justice — the end for which all commonwealths are instituted. This division is what is meant when it is said, 'A kingdom divided in itself cannot stand.' For unless this division comes first, division into opposing armies can never happen. If there had not first been an opinion received among most of England that these powers were divided between the king, the lords, and the House of Commons, the people would never have been divided, nor fallen into this civil war — first between those who disagreed in politics, and afterwards between the dissenters about the liberty of religion. These wars have so instructed men on this point of sovereign right that there are few now (in England) who do not see that these rights are inseparable; and this will be generally acknowledged at the next return of peace, and continue to be acknowledged until their miseries are forgotten — no longer, unless the common people are better taught than they have been until now.

And because these are essential and inseparable rights, it follows necessarily that in whatever words any of them seems to be granted away, if the sovereign power itself is not in direct terms renounced — and if the name of sovereign is no longer given by the grantees to him who grants them — the grant is void. For when he has granted all he can, if we grant the sovereignty back, all is restored, as being inseparably annexed to it.

Since this great authority is indivisible, and inseparably annexed to the sovereignty, there is little ground for the opinion of those who say of sovereign kings that, though they are singulis majores — of greater power than any one of their subjects — they are universis minores, of less power than all of them together. For if by 'all together' they do not mean the collective body taken as one person, then 'all together' and 'each one' mean the same thing, and the saying is absurd. But if by 'all together' they understand it as one person (which person the sovereign bears), then the power of 'all together' is the same as the sovereign's power; and so again the saying is absurd. They see the absurdity well enough when the sovereignty is in an assembly of the people; but in a monarch they do not see it. Yet the power of sovereignty is the same wherever it may be placed.

And as the power, so also the honour of the sovereign ought to be greater than that of any one — or all — of the subjects. For in the sovereignty is the fountain of honour. The dignities of lord, earl, duke, and prince are his creatures. As in the presence of the master, the servants are all equal, and have no honour at all, so are the subjects in the presence of the sovereign. And though they shine, some more, some less, when out of his sight, in his presence they shine no more than the stars in the presence of the sun.
Sovereign power is not as harmful as the lack of it; and the harm that comes from it, for the most part, comes from not readily submitting to a lesser harm.

But here a man may object that the condition of subjects is very miserable, since they are exposed to the lusts and other irregular passions of the man or men who have such unlimited power in their hands. And commonly those who live under a monarch think it the fault of monarchy, and those who live under a democracy or other sovereign assembly attribute every inconvenience to that form of commonwealth — whereas the power, in any of the forms, if they are sufficient to protect the subjects, is the same. They do not consider that the estate of man can never be without some inconvenience or other, and that the greatest that in any form of government can possibly happen to the people in general is scarcely felt, compared with the miseries and horrible calamities that accompany a civil war, or that dissolute condition of masterless men without subjection to laws, and without a coercive power to tie their hands from rapine and revenge. Nor do they consider that the greatest pressure of sovereign governors does not come from any delight or profit they expect from harming or weakening their subjects (in whose vigour their own strength consists), but from the subjects themselves, who, unwillingly contributing to their own defence, make it necessary for their governors to draw from them what they can in time of peace, that they may have means on any sudden emergency to resist or take advantage of their enemies. For all men are by nature equipped with notable magnifying glasses — their passions and self-love — through which every little payment appears a great grievance; but they lack those telescopes (namely moral and civil science) by which they might see at a distance the miseries that hang over them, and that cannot be avoided without such payments.
